transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-12 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Lunaris Head of ML), Sofia Martinez (Eng Manager), Ethan Li (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-generated may be imperfect): Quick review of cost bench marks; question about KV cache vs prefix cache savings; discussion on batching size and tail latency; plan to run 24h benchmark.

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick agenda — cost numbers, caching, batching tradeoffs, next steps. real quick who do we have?
[00:08] Daniel: hey, Daniel here, Daniel Park. we got Sofia and Ethan as well.
[00:12] Sofia: hi all.
[00:14] Ethan: hey.
[00:15] Priya: priya from redwood, i'll run the bench today and share the logs.
[00:20] Jordan: awesome. so follow-up from last week — we ran the 6h cost bench on your small dataset, results look promising but want to talk tokens per dollar. Priya, want to kick off?
[00:30] Priya: yeah. quick caveat transcription might miss some numbers, but baseline hosted run (no cache, batch=1) averaged about 38 tokens/sec per dollar on our A100-style instance profile using fp16. when we enabled prefix caching we saw a jump to ~85 tokens/sec per dollar, and when we combined prefix + KV cache we hit ~120 tokens/sec per dollar for that workload. those are median figures — p50.
[01:02] Daniel: 120 sounds great. can you remind me what you mean by KV cache, i think last time you said key val K over V?
[01:12] Priya: yeah sorry, K/V cache — it's the per-sequence KV cache reuse across similar prompts. so for chat-style prompts that reuse system messages or long context parts it saves recompute. prefix cache is more about template prefixes.
[01:25] Ethan: what was the token mix? ours is heavier on long context — average 900 tokens per request.
[01:33] Priya: right so in your trace the average was 860-920, so KV savings were higher than for short prompts. we also tried batching at sizes 4 and 8. batching 4 improved tokens/sec/$ by about 1.6x over batch=1, batching 8 about 2.4x, but tail latencies increased.
[01:52] Jordan: can you quantify tail?
[01:55] Priya: p95 tail — batch=1 had p95 ~120ms. batch=4 p95 ~190-220ms. batch=8 p95 peaked around 380-420ms on our lab runs. p99 for batch=8 hit 720ms occasionally. so there's a tradeoff — higher throughput, worse tail.
[02:18] Sofia: our SLO is 200ms p95 for user-facing latency, so batch=8 sounds risky. batch=4 maybe ok but depends on distribution.
[02:28] Daniel: what about dedicated? doesn't dedicated reduce latency issue?
[02:31] Jordan: yes Dedicated with pinned GPUs and affinity reduces noisy neighbor variability; we've seen p95 drop ~20-30% vs shared hosted under comparable batch settings. Dedicated also gives you predictable throughput so batching policies can be tuned more aggressively.
[02:46] Daniel: cost-wise how does dedicated compare?
[02:48] Priya: base unit cost is higher for Dedicated reservation but because of consistent utilization you often achieve better tokens/sec/$ for steady high throughput. example — at 90% utilization our estimate is ~145 tokens/sec/$ with prefix+KV cache and batching=4 on Dedicated vs 120 tokens/sec/$ on hosted for the same workload. but committed monthly cost and minimums are factors.
[03:12] Ethan: can you show how cache hit rates looked?
[03:15] Priya: yes hit rates were about 28% for prefix-only on your trace, KV combined raised effective hit to ~52% which is why the combined savings are so big. note these are sensitive to prompt variance.
[03:27] Daniel: is there risk of stale state with KV reuse? like if we rotate system prompts?
[03:31] Priya: good question — KV cache is keyed to the exact KV state and session ID; if you rotate system messages you'd invalidate keys and recompute; we have TTL and explicit invalidation. we'd recommend a TTL aligned with your rollout cadence.
[03:44] Jordan: quick aside — quantization. we ran 4-bit quant on a copy of your model; memory footprint down ~40%, throughput improved slightly on certain kernels but there's a small quality delta. Daniel, you had raised quality sensitivity?
[04:00] Daniel: yes some hallucination tests earlier were slightly worse after aggressive quant, so probably stick to 8-bit for critical paths.
[04:08] Priya: agreed — 8-bit (or q4_0 in our tooling) often gives best sweet spot. we can run evals on your evalset.
[04:15] Sofia: what's the easiest path to test those?
[04:17] Priya: we'll run a branch on our infra with q8 quant and compare on your sample traffic. that's part of the 24h run.
[04:25] Jordan: can we talk about batching policy — is there an auto-batcher or do you want static batch sizes?
[04:31] Priya: our runtime supports continuous batching and latency-aware routing. you can set a latency SLO and it will try dynamic batching up to a max. in practice we run experiments with cap sizes like 4 and 8 and a latency SLO of 200ms p95, the system will bias to smaller batches unless load is high.
[04:48] Ethan: interesting. our traffic is spiky — hourly bursts. will caching still help on spikes?
[04:53] Priya: yes prefix cache helps immediately for repeated prompts; KV helps if session reuse across requests. bursts increase batching opportunities too but tail will spike if load surpasses capacity. that's where autoscaling + burst pool helps.
[05:06] Jordan: any legal/security questions before we move on?
[05:09] Sofia: yes can you share SOC2 artifacts and details on KMS integration?
[05:12] Jordan: yep we'll share SOC2 report and our KMS/HSM integration doc; quick note — Dedicated Private deployments can integrate with customer KMS and on-prem key material if needed.
[05:24] Daniel: latency and data isolation are big reasons we're leaning Dedicated, but cost is blocker.
[05:28] Jordan: understood — that's why we want to run a 24h realistic benchmark and give you numbers for both hosted and dedicated side-by-side.
[05:35] Priya: also want to highlight caching amortizes cost a lot for repeat prompt workloads like yours — your top 20 templates were responsible for ~62% of calls in the trace so caching is high impact.
[05:49] Sofia: can you show the NPV or rough run rate impact? ballpark?
[05:53] Priya: rough back-of-envelope: if you process 10M tokens/day, at 120 tokens/sec/$ that's about $83/day on that profile; if dedicated lifts to 145 tokens/sec/$ that becomes ~$69/day. over a month that's ~4200 vs ~3500. exact numbers depend on utilization and commitment discounts.
[06:14] Daniel: ok that's helpful. what about cache storage costs? are those material?
[06:18] Priya: prefix cache storage is minimal (strings/ids). KV caches are in-memory on the serving node; we account for memory footprint in the pricing model, but there isn't a large separate storage bill.
[06:29] Ethan: for our near-term pilot, what's the recommended config?
[06:32] Priya: i'd recommend hosted initial pilot with prefix+KV caching enabled, batch cap 4 with latency SLO 200ms p95, quantization at 8-bit for model parity, and if after 2 weeks you hit steady throughput above X (we'll define X from your trace) we can propose Dedicated commit options.
[06:49] Jordan: action items recap at the end. but Priya, can you also prepare the raw logs in CSV with tokens/time and batch sizes?
[06:56] Priya: yes will attach to the bench result.
[07:00] Daniel: any comments on multi-region fallbacks? our compliance needs EU data residency for some customers.
[07:06] Jordan: we support region routing and fallbacks; Dedicated can be provisioned in EU region and Private deployments if you need on-prem. if you need data never leaving EU, Private is the recommended path.
[07:18] Sofia: for the security review do you have a template for the info we should prepare?
[07:22] Jordan: yes we'll send a checklist — SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs, data retention settings, pen test, SOC2 report.
[07:29] Ethan: quick nit — you mentioned autoscaling burst pool earlier, can we set a budget for burst cost?
[07:34] Priya: yes you can set a burst cap and threshold; system will prefer using burst credit and then fallback to lower-cost variants or reduce batch sizes.
[07:43] Daniel: are there fallbacks to smaller models to save cost if spike happens?
[07:46] Priya: yes model routing can fallback to a compatible smaller quantized variant; we can configure quality thresholds so you don't fall back for critical flows.
[07:58] Jordan: ok let's surface any open concerns now.
[08:02] Sofia: just want to ensure the tail latency numbers above reflect production-like spikes; the 24h run should capture that.
[08:08] Priya: agreed — we'll include synthetic spike windows.
[08:12] Daniel: curious about measurement methodology — how did you compute tokens/sec/$?
[08:16] Priya: we compute tokens generated per total cost over the run. cost includes GPU + memory amortization + infra overhead. tokens/sec/$ is tokens per second divided by dollars per second, simplified to tokens per dollar across the run. small noise in short runs which is why 24h helps.
[08:33] Jordan: good. any competitor concerns? Daniel?
[08:36] Daniel: some folks internally asked whether we should just use Replicate or SageMaker endpoints; cost wise those are similar but integration and operationaling is why Redwood is attractive. openai is simpler but gives less control and uncertain residency.
[08:54] Priya: and redwood's advantage is runtime optimizations + caching + rollout controls which all help unit economics over time.
[08:59] Sofia: one last question — do you have a recommended eviction TTL for KV keys?
[09:03] Priya: we usually start with 24h TTL for pilot, adjust based on reuse; for nightly retrains you may want to invalidate keys post retrain.
[09:12] Jordan: ok wrapping up. quick recap and next steps.
[09:16] Priya: recap: run 24h bench (prefix-only, KV, batch caps 1/4/8), include spike windows, test q8 quant, produce CSV logs and a summary doc.
[09:26] Jordan: i'll send pricing + SOC2 checklist. Daniel to upload 72h trace. schedule security meeting for next Tue.
[09:34] Daniel: sounds good. thanks all.

Transcript notes: transcription imperfect at times (numbers and acronyms may be slightly off), speaker turns occasionally merged.

End of call.
